# Components and Repetition

A fence has a lot of repeated parts. A deck has more. If each post, joist, and
picket is an independent body, a small design change becomes a long afternoon.
Components and patterns keep one source of truth.

## What you will learn

- The difference between a body, a component, and an occurrence.
- When to use a pattern and when to use a component copy.
- How to lay out repeated parts at fixed spacing.
- How to get a bill of materials from the assembly.

## Bodies, components, and occurrences

A **body** is a solid. A **component** is a definition made of one or more
bodies, plus the features that make them. An **occurrence** is one placement of
that definition in the assembly.

The practical difference: ten copies of a post component are ten occurrences of
one definition. Change the definition, and all ten change. Ten independent post
bodies are ten separate edits.

Use components when:

- the same part appears more than once;
- you want a count in the BOM;
- you may replace the part with a purchased item later;
- you want to move a whole subassembly as a unit.

Use plain bodies when the part is unique or when you are still exploring the
shape.

## Patterns vs copies

Both repeat geometry, but they solve different problems.

| Tool | Best for | Trade-off |
|------|----------|-----------|
| Rectangular pattern | pickets, balusters, studs, joists in one run | Fast; all copies live in one feature |
| Component copies | repeated posts, repeated panels, purchased parts | More control; each occurrence can be counted and moved |
| Mirror | left/right stiles, stringers, brackets | Creates a mirrored definition or body |

A useful rule: if you need to count it, schedule it, or replace it, make it a
component. If it is a simple array inside one part, a pattern is enough.

## Laying out repeated parts

For a run of parts at equal centres, define:

- the start datum;
- the on-centre spacing;
- the count, or the overall length that determines the count.

For example, posts at 2400 mm centres starting at the outside face of the first
post:

- post 1 at 0 mm;
- post 2 at 2400 mm;
- post 3 at 4800 mm.

If the run is 7200 mm and the posts are 90 mm wide, check whether the last post
lands where the drawing says. The difference between centre-to-centre and
clear spacing is a common source of a fence that is one bay short.

## The bill of materials

An assembly can produce a bill of materials: part number, description,
revision, count, and the definition behind each row. Export it as CSV or JSON
when you need to price or order material.

The BOM is not a cut list. It tells you how many of each part; it does not tell
you how to cut them from stock, how much waste to allow, or which offcuts to
reuse. Those are Chapter 9 and Chapter 15 jobs.

## Build along: three fence posts

1. Build one 90 × 90 × 1800 mm post as a component.
2. Place the first occurrence at the datum.
3. Copy it to 2400 mm and 4800 mm centres.
4. Confirm that all three occurrences share one definition.
5. Add a part number and description to the component.
6. Generate the BOM and confirm a count of three.

## Checks

- Three occurrences, one definition.
- Spacing is measured from the same datum for every post.
- The BOM count is three, not one and not six.
- Moving one occurrence does not move the others.
- Editing the definition updates all three.

## Exercises

1. Make nine deck joists at 400 mm centres with a rectangular pattern.
2. Make ten pickets as component copies and confirm the BOM count.
3. Build a gate as one component, then place two copies for a double gate.
4. Deliberately edit one occurrence instead of the definition. What happens to
   the other copies? Which behaviour do you want for this part?
